When reporting a problem, provide detailed information so we can assist you more effectively.\n    31→\n    32→## Setup\n    33→\n    34→Our environment setup is the same as the setup of the official [slime](https://github.com/THUDM/slime) framework. We use Docker:\n    35→\n    36→```bash\n    37→# Pull the image\n    38→docker pull slimerl/slime:v0.5.0rc0-cu126\n    39→\n    40→# Start the container\n    41→docker run -d --gpus all --ipc=host --shm-size=16g \\\n    42→  --ulimit memlock=-1 --ulimit stack=67108864 \\\n    43→  --name RLVE \\\n    44→  slimerl/slime:v0.5.0rc0-cu126 \\\n    45→  tail -f /dev/null\n    46→```\n    47→\n    48→After entering the Docker container, please follow these steps to clone the repository and install it:\n    49→\n    50→```bash\n    51→cd /root/\n    52→git clone https://github.com/Zhiyuan-Zeng/RLVE.git\n    53→cd RLVE\n    54→pip install -e .\n    55→```\n    56→\n    57→## Usage of Verifiable Environments in RLVE-Gym\n    58→\n    59→Each environment has an identifier, which you can find [here](Gym/environments/__init__.py). We take the following example:\n    60→\n    61→```python\n    62→identifier = \"Sorting\"\n    63→```\n    64→\n    65→Each environment has two classes - one for the environment itself and another for controlling the problem difficulty:\n    66→\n    67→```python\n    68→from Gym.environments import identifier2environment\n    69→from Gym.parameter_controllers import identifier2controller\n    70→\n    71→environment = identifier2environment[identifier]\n    72→controller_class = identifier2controller[identifier]\n    73→```\n    74→\n    75→Note that when creating the environment, you can specify the argument `answer_markers` to control how the answer is extracted from a model’s output during verification.\n    76→By default, it extracts the answer enclosed between `<answer>` and `</answer>`.\n    77→You can check [this example usage](slime/rollout/rm_hub/rlve_rm.py) for reference.\n    78→\n    79→When generating a problem, we specify a random seed `seed` and a problem difficulty level `d` ($d \\geq 0$):\n    80→\n    81→```python\n    82→import random\n    83→\n    84→seed = 42\n    85→\n    86→controller = controller_class()\n    87→d = 3\n    88→for _ in range(d) :\n    89→    controller.update()\n    90→\n    91→problem = environment()\n    92→parameter = random.choice(controller.get_parameter_list())\n    93→if problem.generator(seed = seed, parameter = parameter) :\n    94→    pass\n    95→else :\n    96→    problem = None\n    97→```\n    98→\n    99→Problem generation is successful when `problem` is not `None`.\n   100→\n   101→The input prompt is obtained via `problem.prompt_generator()`.  \n   102→The reward for a model output `output` is given by `problem.scorer(output)`, or you can access more detailed verification information using `problem.verifier(output)`.\n   103→\n   104→You can check [here](Gym/environment.py) for more detailed usage.\n   105→\n   106→## Model Download & Weight Conversion\n   107→\n   108→In the following, issues observed on A100 hardware.\n   110→\n   111→We download models from Hugging Face and convert their weights from the Hugging Face format to the Megatron format:\n   112→\n   113→```bash\n 155→**Warning:** Please make sure the weight conversion is successful before starting any training.\n   156→Even if the conversion fails, training can still launch without a runtime error, but the model will be trained from randomly initialized weights.\n   157→\n   158→\n   159→## Reward Shaping\n   160→\n   161→By default, we use the original reward provided by each verifiable environment as the reward used in the RL algorithm.  \n   162→Many environments employ continuous reward shaping, meaning that a model output can still receive a positive reward even if its answer is not fully correct.  \n   163→We found that when the training scale is small, using a binary reward can sometimes yield slightly better results (i.e., the model output receives 1 if and only if its answer is fully correct, and 0 otherwise).  \n   164→You can switch to binary rewards by changing `--reward-key reward` to `--reward-key accuracy` in `scripts/training/[MODEL]/rlve.sh`.\n   165→\n   166→## Wandb Setup\n   167→\n   168→To use Weights & Biases (wandb), please set your wandb API key in the environment variable `WANDB_API_KEY`.  \n   169→Alternatively, you can comment out the wandb-related arguments in `WANDB_ARGS` within the training script to disable wandb.\n   170→\n   171→## Environment Scaling\n   172→\n   173→You can run our environment scaling experiments as follows:\n   174→\n We take the following example:\n\n```python\nidentifier = \"Sorting\"\n```\n\nEach environment has two classes - one for the environment itself and another for controlling the problem difficulty:\n\n```python\nfrom Gym.environments import identifier2environment\nfrom Gym.parameter_controllers import identifier2controller\n\nenvironment = identifier2environment[identifier]\ncontroller_class = identifier2controller[identifier]\n```\n\nNote that when creating the environment, you can specify the argument `answer_markers` to control how the answer is extracted from a model’s output during verification.\nBy default, it extracts the answer enclosed between `<answer>` and `</answer>`.\nYou can check [this example usage](slime/rollout/rm_hub/rlve_rm.py) for reference.\n\nWhen generating a problem, we specify a random seed `seed` and a problem difficulty level `d` ($d \\geq 0$):\n\n```python\nimport random\n\nseed = 42\n\ncontroller = controller_class()\nd = 3\nfor _ in range(d) :\n    controller.update()\n\nproblem = environment()\nparameter = random.choice(controller.get_parameter_list())\nif problem.generator(seed = seed, parameter = parameter) :\n    pass\nelse :\n    problem = None\n```\n\nProblem generation is successful when `problem` is not `None`.\n\nThe input prompt is obtained via `problem.prompt_generator()`.  \nThe reward for a model output `output` is given by `problem.scorer(output)`, or you can access more detailed verification information using `problem.verifier(output)`.\n\nYou can check [here](Gym/environment.py) for more detailed usage.\n\n## Model Download & Weight Conversion\n\nIn the following, we assume you are on a node with 8 GPUs, each verifiable environment as the reward used in the RL algorithm.  \nMany environments employ continuous reward shaping, meaning that a model output can still receive a positive reward even if its answer is not fully correct.  \nWe found that when the training scale is small, using a binary reward can sometimes yield slightly better results (i.e., the model output receives 1 if and only if its answer is fully correct, and 0 otherwise).  \nYou can switch to binary rewards by changing `--reward-key reward` to `--reward-key accuracy` in `scripts/training/[MODEL]/rlve.sh`.\n\n## Wandb
